q: Sound, as defined in the lecture, is which kind of wave?
why: A speaker vibrates back and forth, compressing and expanding air, producing a longitudinal pressure wave.

q: Why is there no sound in outer space?
choices: There is no air to compress
The frequency there is too high
Space is too cold for waves
why: Sound is molecules of air being compressed and expanded; without air there is no sound.

q: Bending of a sound wave around an obstacle is called:
why: Reflection = bouncing, refraction = change of angle entering a denser medium, diffraction = bending around an obstacle.

q: A transducer used to detect sound converts:
why: Sound is measured as pressure at a point, using a transducer to convert pressure to voltage levels.

q: Which is NOT one of the three major components of a multimedia system?
why: The three components are content creation, compression/storage, and delivery/distribution.

q: Which is NOT listed as an advantage of digital over analog?
why: Digital has many advantages, but quantization always introduces error.

q: Typical audio sampling rates range from:
why: Audio is sampled at 8-48 kHz; 20 Hz-20 kHz is the hearing range.

q: Human hearing extends from about:
why: The ear hears about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; above that is ultrasound.

q: Analog-to-digital conversion consists of:
why: Two main processes: sampling and quantization.

q: Converting a digital signal back to analog is called:
why: The reverse process (D/A) is known as interpolation.

q: A signal has frequency 250 Hz. Its period is:
A 1 kHz tone travels at 340 m/s. Its wavelength is:
A signal that does not change at all has frequency:
why: No change = zero frequency; an instantaneous change = infinite frequency.

q: If the sampling period T is reduced, then:
why: Reducing T (raising f) increases the number of samples and the storage requirement.

q: A signal range R = 8 V quantized with 4 bits has step size:
Going from 3 bits to 5 bits changes the step size Δ by a factor of:
why: Δ = R/2^b; two more bits divide Δ by 2^2 = 4.

q: At least how many bits are needed for 1000 quantization levels?
Quantization always introduces error because:
choices: The sampling rate is set too low
why: Each sample is represented by a finite number of bits, so the quantized value differs from the actual value.

q: Per the slides, music must be quantized with ___ bits and speech with ___ bits.
why: Audio for music needs 16 bits; speech requires only 8.

q: Uniform quantization works best when:
choices: The signal is mostly very loud
why: Uniform intervals spread the error evenly when all values in the range are equally likely; otherwise use non-linear (log) scales.

q: Bit rate equals:
why: Bits/second = (samples/second) × (bits/sample).

q: Speech sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample has a bit rate of:
why: 8000 × 8 = 64 000 bit/s (professor's table).

q: Mono CD audio (44.1 kHz, 16 bits) has a bit rate of about:
why: 44 100 × 16 = 705 600 bit/s; stereo doubles it to 1.4 Mbps.

q: Stereo CD audio (44.1 kHz, 16 bits) has a bit rate of about:
AM radio at 11 kHz and 8 bits per sample produces:
A 10-second mono clip at 8 kHz, 8 bits takes how many bytes?
Any LTI system is fully characterised by its:
why: The output is the input convolved with the impulse response.

q: In the time domain, the output of an LTI system is:
choices: Input multiplied by its own transfer function
Input sampled at the Nyquist rate
why: Time-domain view: output = input * impulse response (convolution).

q: Convolution f*g integrates f multiplied by g that has been:
why: Convolution = integral of the first signal multiplied with the other signal reversed and shifted.

q: The Dirac delta function is zero everywhere except x = 0, and its integral is:
why: A sharp peak bounding unit area: infinite at x = 0, integral 1.

q: The sampling theorem was established by ___ and formalised by ___ in 1950.
why: Henry Nyquist (late 1920s), formalised by Claude Shannon in 1950.

q: A signal's maximum frequency is 10 kHz. It must be sampled at more than:
why: f_s > 2 × f_max = 20 kHz, the Nyquist sampling frequency (professor's example).

q: Speech band-limited to 4 kHz needs a sampling rate above:
why: 2 × 4 kHz = 8 kHz, matching the 8 kHz telephone rate.

q: A signal contains 2 kHz, 5 kHz and 7.5 kHz. Its Nyquist sampling frequency is:
why: Only the highest component matters: 2 × 7.5 kHz = 15 kHz.

q: Sampling well above the Nyquist frequency causes:
why: Oversampling reproduces the signal correctly but creates extra storage and transmission overhead.

q: Aliasing is:
choices: Random noise added by analog circuits
why: Aliasing describes loss of information when sampling below the Nyquist frequency.

q: A 9 kHz tone sampled at 8 kHz is heard as:
why: |9 - 8| = 1 kHz, below f_s/2 = 4 kHz.

q: The wagon wheel turning backwards in western films is an example of:
why: The movie camera has undersampled the wheels' motion in time.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: SNR is the ratio of:
why: The ratio of the power of the correct signal to the noise; a measure of signal quality.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: V_signal is 10 times V_noise. The SNR is:
why: 20 × log10(10) = 20 dB (the professor's example).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Signal power is 1000 times noise power. The SNR is:
why: For power use 10·log10: 10 × 3 = 30 dB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Why does SNR use 20·log10 for voltages?
choices: Power is proportional to V squared
Noise always has two equal components
why: Power ∝ V², so 10·log10(V²) = 20·log10(V).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Quantization noise is the difference between the analog value and:
choices: The noise measured on the analog line
why: Defined against the nearest quantization interval value at the sampling instant.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Quantization error is at most:
why: At most, the error can be as much as half of the interval.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The SQNR formula for a sinusoidal input is:
why: SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB, N = bits per sample.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The slide's maximum SQNR for 16-bit audio is about:
why: 6.02 × 16 = 96.3 dB; each bit adds about 6 dB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Using 6.02N, the SQNR of 8-bit audio is about:

q: Using 6.02N + 1.76, the SQNR of 16-bit audio is:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Going from 12 to 16 bits per sample improves SQNR by about:
why: 4 extra bits × 6.02 dB = 24.08 dB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Minimum bits for SQNR ≥ 75 dB using 6.02N:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76, the symbol N is:
why: Here N is bits. On L2 slide 29, N = 2^b means levels; do not mix them.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: For speech, the frequencies typically retained are:
why: Speech 50 Hz-10 kHz; music about 20 Hz-20 kHz.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The filter screening out both low and high frequencies at the encoder is a:
why: A bandpass (band-limiting) filter screens out lower and higher frequencies.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Which filter is applied after the DAC at the decoder?
why: High frequencies reappear through sampling and quantization, so a low-pass filter with the encoder's high cutoff is used.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Compared with mono, stereo audio needs:
why: Stereo information doubles the bitrate needed.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In computer networking, 'bandwidth' means:
choices: A data rate in bits per second
The number of quantization bits used
why: For analog devices bandwidth is in Hz; in networking it is the data rate in bps.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Table 6.2 lists CD audio as 176.4 kB/s. In kbps that is:
why: kB/s are bytes: 176.4 × 8 = 1411.2 kbps = 44.1 kHz × 16 × 2.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: How many bytes does one minute of CD-quality stereo audio take?
why: 1 411 200 bit/s × 60 s ÷ 8 = 10 584 000 bytes, the slide's 'about 10 MB'.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The two approaches to handling stored sampled audio are:
why: FM (frequency modulation) and Wave Table (Wave) sound.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: MIDI files are very small because MIDI:
why: MIDI is a scripting language: it codes events such as pitch, volume and instrument.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Per the slide, 3 minutes of music stored as MIDI messages takes about:
why: 3 minutes in about 3 kB, versus WAV storing 1 minute in about 10 MB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: How many MIDI channels are there?
why: 16 channels, numbered 0-15, carried in the low 4 bits of the status byte.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The MIDI channel number occupies which bits of the status byte?
why: The channel is the last four (least significant) bits.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In General MIDI, channel 10 is reserved for:
why: Channel 10 is reserved for percussion instruments (drums).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Messages that carry no channel number and address all instruments are:
why: System messages, e.g. a change in tuning or timing, go to all instruments.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: A MIDI keyboard on its own:
why: It generates MIDI messages; it may also include a synthesizer.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Timbre is:
choices: The loudness envelope of a note
why: Timbre is what instrument is emulated, e.g. piano vs violin: the quality of the sound.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: '16-part multi-timbral' means a module can play:
why: Multi-timbral = different instrument sounds at once; polyphony counts simultaneous notes.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: '64 voices of polyphony' means a module can play:
why: Polyphony is the number of voices (notes) produced at the same time.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In MIDI, a 'voice' is:
choices: Each timbre and pitch at once
A system message sent to all channels
why: Every different timbre and pitch the tone module can produce at the same time.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The set of control settings that defines a particular timbre is a:
why: A patch defines a timbre; patches are organised into databases called banks.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: General MIDI defines how many patches for standard instruments?
why: 128 patches; plus a percussion map of 47 sounds.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: A General MIDI device must have at least how many dynamically allocated voices?
why: It must support all 16 channels, be multi-timbral and polyphonic, and have at least 24 voices.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: A MIDI status byte has a value between:
why: Status bytes have MSB = 1 (128-255); data bytes have MSB = 0 (0-127).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: How many bits does one MIDI byte occupy on the wire?
why: 8 data bits plus a 0 start bit and a stop bit.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Status byte 0x93 means:
why: High nibble 9 = Note On (&H9n); low nibble n = 3.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Status byte 0xC5 is:
why: &HCn = program change; n = 5. Control change is &HBn, pitch bend &HEn.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Note On for the drum channel (channel 10 counted from 1) has status byte:
why: Channels are numbered 0-15 in the byte, so channel 10 is n = 9: 0x99.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The MIDI serial connection runs at:
why: A 31.25 kbps serial link with 10-bit bytes.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: MIDI communication is:
why: The slide states MIDI communication is half-duplex.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The MIDI THRU port:
why: THRU simply copies data entering the IN channel, for daisy-chaining.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: One 3-byte MIDI note message takes about:
why: 30 bits / 31 250 bit/s = 0.00096 s. (0.77 ms wrongly uses 8-bit bytes.)

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Ten Note On plus ten Note Off messages take about:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Recording one sound through several bandpass filters and mapping each to keys is:
why: Multisampling makes pitch shifting more reliable, since less shift is needed per note.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Quantization and transformation of data together are known as:
why: Quantization and transformation are collectively known as coding of the data.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The three stages of every compression scheme, in order, are:
why: 1 transformation, 2 loss (quantization), 3 coding (codewords).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The main lossy step in a compression scheme is:
why: Quantization uses fewer reconstruction levels than the original, so information is lost.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Huffman coding belongs to which compression stage?
why: The coding stage assigns codewords, fixed- or variable-length such as Huffman.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In the PCM decoder chain, what follows the µ-law/A-law expander?
why: Figure 6.15: DAC → expander → low-pass filter → output analog speech.

q: In AM (amplitude modulation), which property of the carrier is varied?
why: AM varies the carrier's height to carry the data; FM varies frequency, PM varies phase.

q: In a quantizer, the set of input-interval boundaries that map to the same output level is the:
why: Boundaries form the coder mapping; the representative output values form the decoder mapping.

q: What are the three stages of every compression scheme, in order?
why: Transform to an easier representation, introduce loss (quantization), then assign codewords.

q: Which stage is the main lossy step in compression?
why: Quantization uses fewer reconstruction levels than the original, so information is necessarily lost.

q: How is the compression ratio defined?
choices: B0 − B1 (the number of bits saved)
why: Compression ratio = B0/B1, and a good codec has a ratio much larger than 1.

q: Self-information log2(1/p_i) corresponds to:
choices: The bits needed to encode symbol s_i
The probability of the symbol s_i
The average code length of the whole code
why: Shannon's self-information is the ideal number of bits for that symbol.

q: Entropy of an image whose 256 grey levels are all equally likely?
The two-valued image on slide 13 has entropy about:
why: With p = 1/3 and 2/3, η ≈ 0.918 ≈ 0.92, under 1 bit.

q: Entropy of a source with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8?
Self-information of a symbol with p = 1/8?
why: log2(1/(1/8)) = log2 8 = 3. (0.375 is p·log2(1/p), its contribution to η.)

q: Entropy of the string HELLO, roughly?
why: 0.4·1.32 + 3·0.2·2.32 ≈ 1.922. 2.0 is the Huffman average, not η.

q: For HELLO the slide's 'log2' column shows 1.32 for L. What is it?
choices: The code length given to L
The entropy of the whole string
why: log2(5/2) = 1.32 is L's self-information, not its actual code length (1 bit).

q: Which value can the entropy of an n-symbol source NOT exceed?
why: η ≤ log2 n, with equality only for a uniform distribution.

q: A memoryless source is one where:
choices: Each symbol is independent of earlier ones
Symbols always come in long runs
The dictionary is rebuilt for every symbol
Every symbol has exactly the same probability
why: Memoryless = independently distributed; the current symbol does not depend on previous ones.

q: Run-length coding exploits:
why: RLC encodes a symbol plus the length of its continuous group.

q: RLC of BBBBEEEEEEEECCCCDAAAAA?
why: Runs are 4 B, 8 E, 4 C, 1 D, 5 A, written count-then-symbol.

q: 22 characters RLC-encode to 4B8E4C1D5A. Ratio in characters?
RLC-encoding ABCABC (count + symbol) gives how many characters?
why: 1A1B1C1A1B1C, twice the input: RLC expands data without runs.

q: Shannon-Fano coding is a:
why: It sorts symbols and recursively splits them into halves of equal count.

q: After sorting by count, Shannon-Fano repeatedly:
choices: Splits the list into two near-equal-count parts
Merges the two lowest-count symbols together
Adds the current string to a dictionary
Narrows an interval inside [0, 1) after each symbol
why: Recursive division into two parts of about equal total count until each part has one symbol.

q: Why does the slide show two Shannon-Fano trees for HELLO?
choices: The splits are not unique; both are valid
The second tree fixes an error in the first
One is Shannon-Fano and the other Huffman
One tree is the encoder's, one the decoder's
why: Different equally balanced splits are legal; here both give 10 bits.

q: Counts A15 B7 C6 D6 E5: Shannon-Fano needs 89 bits. Huffman needs:
why: Huffman gives A 1 bit and the rest 3 bits: 15 + 24·3 = 87, beating Shannon-Fano.

q: Each Huffman step combines:
choices: The first and the last symbols
Any two adjacent entries in the list
why: Pick the two smallest (leaf or parent), make them siblings under a parent with the summed probability.

q: Must the leaves be sorted before building a Huffman tree?
why: Slide 25: leaves can be sorted, 'though this is not necessary'.

q: Fixed-length code for 6 distinct symbols needs how many bits each?
why: ⌈log2 6⌉ = 3: bits must be whole.

q: Huffman codes L=0, H=10, E=110, O=111 for HELLO. Average code length?
why: 10 bits / 5 symbols = 2.0.

q: Slide 29: after iteration (a) the list is L P1 H. Which symbols formed P1?
why: P1 merges the two count-1 symbols E and O; H stays in the list.

q: Huffman for a: 1/2, b: 1/4, c: 1/8, d: 1/8. Average length?
why: Lengths 1,2,3,3 → 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75, exactly the entropy.

q: MISSISSIPPI (I4 S4 P2 M1) Huffman-coded takes how many bits?
why: Lengths 1 and 2 for S and I, 3 for P and M: 4+8+6+3 = 21 (fixed 2-bit = 22).

q: SHAHZODA (H2 A2, S Z O D 1 each) Huffman-coded takes:
why: H, A get 2 bits, the four singles 3 bits: 8 + 12 = 20 (2.5 bits/letter = η).

q: Code lengths 1,2,3,4,4 for p = .4,.2,.2,.1,.1. Average length?
why: .4 + .4 + .6 + .4 + .4 = 2.2. A tree with lengths 2,2,2,3,3 also gives 2.2.

q: Two students build different Huffman trees for the same source (ties broken differently). Then:
choices: Both are optimal, with equal average length
Only the one with sorted leaves is correct
The one with the shorter longest code wins
Their codes give different compression ratios
why: Tie-breaking changes codes and even code lengths, but the average length is the same minimum.

q: The unique prefix property means:
choices: No codeword is a prefix of another
Every codeword starts with the same bit
Every codeword has exactly the same length
Codewords are sorted by their prefix
why: It precludes ambiguity in decoding, so no separators are needed.

q: In an optimal Huffman code, the two least frequent symbols:
choices: Have equal length, differing in the last bit
Get the two shortest codewords in the code
Always get the codes 0 and 1 respectively
Differ from each other in their very first bit
why: They are siblings at the deepest level, so same length, last bit differs.

q: Huffman's average code length L̄ satisfies:
why: Eq. 7.6: within one bit of the entropy, never below it.

q: A source has η = 2.3 bits. Which Huffman average length is impossible?
why: L̄ must lie in [2.3, 3.3); 3.4 is outside the bound.

q: Is the code a=0, b=01, c=10 uniquely decodable?
choices: Yes: all its codewords are different
Yes: it has fewer than four symbols
No: c is longer than both a and b
why: 0 is a prefix of 01, so the bitstream is ambiguous.

q: Efficiency of a code with η = 1.922 and L̄ = 2.0?
Why is plain Huffman wasteful when one p_i is very large?
choices: Codes must be whole bits, at least 1
It cannot code more than 2 symbols
The tree grows deeper than log2 n
The prefix property no longer holds for it
why: The ideal length log2(1/p_i) is near 0, but Huffman still spends at least 1 bit.

q: p(A)=0.9, p(B)=0.1, Huffman on pairs gives 1.29 bits per pair. Bits per symbol?
What does the slide say about extended Huffman's gain?
choices: It is worse than plain Huffman
It removes the need for a tree
why: Better than plain Huffman but modest, and n^k tables get huge for k ≥ 3.

q: For adaptive Huffman to decode correctly, the encoder and decoder must:
choices: Use the same initial_code and update_tree
Exchange the whole tree after every symbol
Use different trees for odd and even symbols
Agree only on the final frequency counts
why: If the routines differ, the trees diverge and decoding fails.

q: When a swap is needed, which node is swapped with the node just incremented to N+1?
choices: The farthest node with count N
The nearest node with count N+1
The root node of the whole tree
The leaf with the smallest count
why: Swap rule: the farthest node with count N is swapped with the node whose count became N+1.

q: LZW uses:
choices: Variable-length codes for each single symbol
One real number for the whole of the input message
why: Fixed-length codewords represent variable-length strings that occur together.

q: How does the LZW decoder get the dictionary?
choices: It rebuilds it dynamically from the codes
The encoder sends it before the data
It is fixed by the standard in advance, like ASCII
It is stored at the end of the file
why: Encoder and decoder build the same dictionary as the data flows.

q: Which is NOT an advantage of LZW over Huffman listed on the slide?
choices: It is lossy, so it gets higher ratios
No prior knowledge of the data needed
It compresses the data in a single pass
Better on files with repetitive data
why: LZW is lossless; the other three are listed advantages (plus 60–70% on some text).

q: In LZW compression, if s + c is already in the dictionary:
choices: Set s = s + c; output nothing
Add s + c again with a new code
why: Only extend the current string; output and add happen when s + c is new.

q: LZW of ABABBABCABABBA with 1=A, 2=B, 3=C outputs:
why: The slide's trace: 9 codes for 14 characters.

q: In the slide example, what is code 6?
why: s=AB, c=B → output 4, add 6 = ABB.

q: The last dictionary entry made for ABABBABCABABBA is:
why: s=ABB, c=A → output 6, add 11 = ABBA; then A is output at EOF.

q: Slide ratio for 14 characters sent as 9 codes?
why: 14/9 = 1.56 (counting symbols, not bits).

q: LZW of BABAABAAA with 1=A, 2=B outputs:
why: Entries 3=BA, 4=AB, 5=BAA, 6=ABA, 7=AA; the final s = AA is output as 7.

q: Decoder state: s = AB, next code 5 is not yet in the dictionary. Entry = ?
why: Exception handler: entry = s + s[0] = AB + A.

q: Decode 1 2 3 5 with 1=A, 2=B:
why: A, B (3=AB), AB (4=BA), 5 missing → AB+A = ABA. Total ABABABA.

q: When does the LZW decoder's exception handler fire?
choices: A code arrives before the decoder made it
A code is larger than the max code length
The input contains a symbol not in the initial table
why: The decoder is one step behind; if the encoder uses a just-created code, the decoder lacks it.

q: In LZW decoding, the new entry added is:
choices: s + first character of the entry
The current entry on its own
s + the last character of the current entry
why: Algorithm 7.3: add s + entry[0].

q: An LZW dictionary starts with code length l0 = 9. Its initial size?
why: 2^l0 = 2^9 = 512; when full, l grows by 1.

q: Why does arithmetic coding usually beat Huffman?
choices: It is not limited to whole bits per symbol
It uses a fixed-length code for each symbol
It builds a dictionary of long strings
It throws away the inaudible information
why: Huffman uses integer-length codewords; arithmetic coding treats the whole message as one unit.

q: In arithmetic coding a message is represented by:
choices: A binary tree of symbol codewords
A list of indices into a string dictionary
A run count followed by a symbol
why: The interval starts as [0, 1) and narrows with each symbol.

q: The slide's encoder updates low first, then high = low + range·Range_high. What goes wrong?
choices: high uses the new low; both need the old
Nothing; this is the correct update order
range must be updated before low is
why: Compute both bounds from the old low (and old range); the worked table follows that rule.

q: CAEE$: after C then A, the interval is:
CAEE$: after C, A, E, the interval is:
Final interval for CAEE$?
Final range for CAEE$ (p = 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.1)?
why: The final range is the product of the probabilities: 0.2·0.2·0.3·0.3·0.1.

q: Codeword chosen for CAEE$?
why: 0.01010101₂ = 0.33203125, the shortest binary fraction inside [0.33184, 0.3322).

q: How many bits does the CAEE$ codeword use?
why: 0.01010101 has 8 fraction bits.

q: Procedure 7.2 sets the next bit to 1, then changes it back to 0 when:
choices: The value is still below low
why: Set a 1; if value > high, replace by 0; stop once value ≥ low.

q: Decoding 0.33203125: after outputting C [0.3, 0.5), the next value is:
Decoder: value 0.8359375 lies in E [0.55, 0.85). The next value?
Table A [0,.4) B [.4,.7) C [.7,.9) $ [.9,1). Interval after C then A?
Same table: decode the value 0.7545.
Two different numbers inside the final interval [low, high) are decoded. They give:
choices: An error for one of them
why: Any value in the final interval identifies the message; the codeword is just the shortest binary one.

q: Lossy compression gives:
choices: A close approximation, much higher ratio
An exact copy at a much higher ratio
An exact copy at a much lower ratio
A close approximation, at a lower ratio than lossless
why: The output is not identical, but the ratio is much higher than lossless.

q: A 3-bit uniform quantizer covers [−4, 4). Step size?
Data rate of 44.1 kHz, 16-bit stereo audio?
The slide says '84M per minute' for CD audio. 84M of what?
why: 1.4112 Mbit/s × 60 ≈ 84.7 Mbit; in bytes it's about 10.6 MB.

q: CD audio (1,411.2 kbit/s) coded as MP3 at 128 kbit/s. Compression ratio?
Which of these is a lossless audio format?
why: FLAC and Apple Lossless are lossless, at the cost of larger files.

q: MP3 and AAC are both based on:
why: Both are lossy and use the modified discrete cosine transform plus psychoacoustics.

q: The human ear is most sensitive between:
why: Intermediate frequencies, where the basilar membrane reacts most. The hearing range is 20 Hz–20 kHz.

q: Masking is:
choices: One sound reducing perception of another
Adding noise to cover up the quiet passages of a song
why: A strong sound makes nearby (in frequency or time) weaker sounds inaudible.

q: A loud sound hides quieter sounds just before and after it. This is:
why: Temporal masking acts in time; frequency masking acts on nearby frequencies.

q: About how much SNR does each added bit give?
why: Each bit doubles the levels → about 6 dB more SNR; 16 bits ≈ 96 dB.

q: Why does masking allow compression?
choices: Raising the masked noise floor saves bits
Masked bands are then coded losslessly
It removes the need for a filter bank
It doubles the effective sampling rate of the signal
why: Noise under the mask is inaudible; a higher noise floor means fewer bits.

q: Sampling frequencies supported by MPEG-1 audio?
why: Precision 16 bits; sampling 32/44.1/48 kHz.

q: MPEG-1 Layer III (MP3) bit-rate range and target?
Which layer is the dominant standard for DAB radio and DVB TV?
why: MP2, from MUSICAM, is a time-domain sub-band coder used in broadcasting.

q: How many sub-bands does the MPEG audio filter bank produce?
why: The filter bank divides the input into 32 equal-frequency sub-bands.

q: Which order matches the MPEG audio encoder?
choices: Filter bank, psychoacoustic model, bit allocation, bitstream
Psychoacoustic model, bitstream, filter bank, bit allocation
Bit allocation, filter bank, bitstream, psychoacoustic model
Filter bank, bitstream, bit allocation, psychoacoustic model
why: Split into sub-bands, find what is masked, allocate bits, pack the bitstream.

q: MPEG bit allocation computes MNR as:
why: Mask-to-noise ratio = signal-to-noise ratio − signal-to-mask ratio.

q: Each iteration, bits are given to the sub-band with:
why: Lowest MNR = most audible noise, so it needs bits most.

q: SNR = 18 dB, SMR = 12 dB. MNR?
why: MNR = SNR − SMR = 18 − 12.

q: Bands with SMR 12, 3, 20, 8 dB all start at 0 bits. Which band gets the first bit?
why: MNR = 0 − SMR: band 3 has the lowest MNR (−20).

q: Pre-echo is:
choices: Sound heard before it actually occurs
An echo added after every loud sound
Noise above 20 kHz that gets removed
A delay between the two stereo channels
why: A transform-coding artifact most noticeable on percussion like cymbals.

q: Which two artifacts appear at too-low bit-rates?
why: Compression artifacts named on the slide are ringing and pre-echo.

q: AAC was introduced in 1997 as:
why: Introduced as MPEG-2 Part 7, folded into MPEG-4 in 1999.

q: Which is an AAC improvement over MP3?
choices: Pure MDCT filter bank, 8–96 kHz rates
A fixed 128 kbps rate and 32 sub-bands
Lossless coding of all audio content
why: AAC adds more sampling rates, arbitrary bit-rates, variable frame length and a simpler pure-MDCT filter bank.

q: Which MPEG-4 coder targets speech at 6–24 kbps?
why: Code-excited linear prediction: 6–24 kbps at 8/16 kHz. Parametric is 2–6 kbps.

q: MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 14) is:
why: A wrapper holding video and audio streams plus metadata.

q: Scotopic vision uses which receptors?
why: Scotopic (dim-light) vision uses rods only, so objects appear black and white.

q: The Weber ratio is defined as…
why: ΔI is the just-noticeable increment over a background of intensity I.

q: A SMALL Weber ratio means…
why: If a small relative change is already visible, discrimination is good.

q: I = 50, ΔI just visible at 5. Weber ratio?
Seeing the same grey as darker on a bright background is called…
why: Perceived intensity is not a simple function of actual intensity.

q: Over/undershoot bands seen at a sharp intensity edge are…
why: Mach bands show the eye exaggerates edges.

q: A LONGER focal length gives…
why: Longer focal length narrows the angle of view and magnifies.

q: Typical range of visible light?
why: Speaker notes: the eye detects roughly 380-700 nm.

q: In f(x,y) = i(x,y)·r(x,y), r is…
why: i = illumination, r = reflectance.

q: g(x,y) = T[f(x,y)] is a point operation when the neighbourhood is…
why: A 1×1 neighbourhood means s = T(r).

q: Quantization digitises…
why: Sampling digitises coordinates, quantization digitises amplitude.

q: Bits for a 1024 × 1024 image with 256 grey levels?
8192 × 8192, k = 8 (circled on the slide). How many bits?
256 × 256 image with 16 grey levels. Size in bytes?
Storage of an M × N image with L levels is…
why: b = M·N·k with k = log₂L; using L directly is a classic mistake.

q: Too few grey levels in a smooth region causes…
why: Low intensity resolution gives banding (false contouring).

q: Isopreference curves vary which two quantities?
choices: Hue and saturation of the colour
why: Speaker notes: changing N and k independently.

q: According to isopreference curves, images with more detail…
choices: Need more pixels, not more levels
why: Detailed images hide false contouring, so fewer levels are acceptable.

q: The slides' image negative formula is…
why: Negative s = (L−1) − r, written y = −x + 255.

q: Negative of 8-bit pixel 77?
Negative of 3-bit pixel 5?
Threshold T = 128 (≥ T → 255). Pixel 127 becomes?
why: 127 < 128, so it goes to 0.

q: Posterizing to 2 grey levels is the same as…
why: Slide 46: thresholding results when levels are reduced to 2.

q: A bounded threshold…
choices: Thresholds a limited range, passes others through
Thresholds every pixel at two values
Sets every pixel outside a range to 255
Uses a threshold chosen by the histogram
why: Other pixels get the null transform.

q: Stretch with low = 100, high = 151: pixel 130 becomes?
Stretch with low = 100, high = 151: pixel 160 becomes?
why: 160 ≥ high, so it is clipped to 255.

q: 4-bit image, x_min = 4, x_max = 9. Stretched value of x = 7?
Gamma γ < 1 (e.g. 0.45) makes the image…
why: (r)^0.45 > r for 0 < r < 1, so dark tones are lifted.

q: Gamma γ = 2.2 makes the image…
why: γ > 1 pushes mid-tones down.

q: Normalised r = 0.25 with γ = 0.5. Output?
8-bit r = 100, γ = 2.2. Output s (rounded)?
Which pixel values are unchanged by ANY gamma?
why: 0^γ = 0 and 1^γ = 1 after normalising.

q: Why is gamma correction needed?
choices: Cameras are linear but eyes/displays follow a power curve
Cameras record in a power curve but displays are linear
It compresses the file size of displayed images
It removes noise introduced by the sensor array
why: It prevents bleaching or darkening on different monitors.

q: 173 = 10101101₂. 2-bit bit clipping gives?
Bit plane 7 of an 8-bit image looks like…
why: Bit 7 is 1 exactly when r ≥ 128.

q: Log transform s = c·log₁₀(1+r), c = 105.89. r = 99?
A narrow histogram bunched to the left means…
why: Left = dark; narrow = low contrast.

q: Row-major index of row 2, column 3 in a 5-wide image (0-based)?
Column-major index of row 2, column 3 in a 4-high image?
Radiometry measures…
choices: Radiation across the whole optical spectrum
Only visible light weighted by the eye
Only the perceived brightness of a source
Only the colour of reflected light
why: Photometry is the eye-weighted visible part.

q: Luminance (lumens) measures…
choices: Energy an observer perceives from a source
Total energy flowing from the source
why: Radiance = total energy (W); luminance = perceived (lm).

q: Which quantity is 'practically impossible to measure'?
why: Brightness is a subjective descriptor.

q: Photopic sensitivity peaks at…
why: Yellow-green, 555 nm; half at 510 and 610 nm.

q: Scotopic sensitivity peaks at…
why: Blue-green, 507 nm.

q: ND(p) of p = (x, y) is…
why: The four diagonal neighbours.

q: Which pixel is in N4 of (3, 5)?
why: N4 changes exactly one coordinate by 1.

q: The slide's 8-connectivity definition says q ∈ N4(p). This is…
choices: A typo: it should be N8(p)
why: As written it duplicates the 4-connectivity definition.

q: Diagonal q is m-adjacent to p only if…
choices: N4(p) ∩ N4(q) has no pixel in V
N4(p) ∩ N4(q) has a pixel in V
why: This removes the duplicate diagonal route.

q: m-connectivity was introduced to…
why: 8-connectivity can join two pixels by two routes.

q: V = {1}, grid 011/010/001. How many 8-paths from centre to top-right?
why: Direct diagonal, and via (0,1). m allows only the latter.

q: Length n of a path (x₀,y₀) … (xₙ,yₙ) counts…
why: n+1 pixels give a path of length n.

q: Of a region's boundaries, which is always a closed path?
why: The inner boundary need not close; the outer one does.

q: p = (0,0), q = (4,4). D8 (chessboard)?
p = (0,0), q = (4,4). Euclidean distance?
p = (1,6), q = (4,2). Euclidean distance?
How many pixels have D4 ≤ 1 from a centre (including it)?
why: Centre + its 4 N4 neighbours.

q: How many pixels have D8 ≤ 2 from a centre?
why: A 5×5 square.

q: Which distance depends on the pixel VALUES along the way?
why: D4, D8, D_E use coordinates only.

q: Slide 34 case p1=0, p3=0 (V={1}). m-distance p→p4?
why: Both diagonals are allowed: p, p2, p4.

q: Triangle inequality for a metric D:
why: The other true ones are non-negativity and symmetry.

q: For any two pixels, which ordering always holds?
why: max ≤ √(sum of squares) ≤ sum.

q: Gonzalez grid, V = {0,1}: shortest m-path p→q is 5 and 8-path is…
Image arithmetic requires the images to…
why: Operations are element-wise.

q: HSI separates colour from…
why: Hue and saturation carry colour; I carries brightness.

q: In CIE XYZ, Y represents…
why: Y matches the eye's brightness sensitivity.

q: X = 20, Y = 30, Z = 50. Chromaticity x?
Chromaticity x = 0.3, y = 0.4. What is z?
In polar chromaticity around the white point, the angle is…
why: Angle = hue, radius = saturation/purity.

q: Gamut is…
choices: The subset of colours a device can reproduce
The brightest colour a display can produce
The number of grey levels in an image
The wavelength of the dominant colour
why: On the chromaticity diagram it is the primaries' triangle.

q: Lines of resolution: NTSC vs PAL?
why: NTSC 525, PAL 625.

q: Light with equal amounts of all wavelengths is…
why: Monochromatic = one wavelength (laser); polychromatic = unequal mix.

q: RGB (200, 100, 50) to 8-bit CMY?
HSI intensity of RGB (200, 100, 50)?
CIE criterion for XYZ: equal amounts of the primaries produce…
why: X = Y = Z gives the equal-energy white point (1/3, 1/3).

q: Bits per pixel of an 8-bit-per-channel RGB image?
In a LUT, the current pixel value is used as…
why: New value = LUT[old value].

q: LUT = [0,0,1,1,2,3,4,5]. Input 7 becomes?
why: LUT[7] is the last entry, 5.

q: Main storage advantage of a colormap:
choices: It increases the number of colours shown
It makes images lossless in compression
why: Only the 8-bit index is stored per pixel.

q: 256×256 indexed image + 256-entry RGB LUT. Total bytes?
Multiplying an image by 1.2 does what to its histogram?
why: ×1.2 spreads values; ÷1.2 squeezes them.

q: Goal of histogram equalisation:
why: Specification targets a chosen shape; equalisation targets uniform.

q: The HE transform T(r) is the input's…
why: s = ∫₀ʳ p_r(w) dw.

q: T(r) must be single-valued and…
why: So it is invertible and keeps the order of levels.

q: Why is a discrete equalised histogram NOT flat?
choices: Levels can merge but never split
why: All pixels at one level map to one output level.

q: HE stretches contrast near histogram…
why: Contrast is compressed near minima.

q: Slide 30: 16 pixels, L = 8, cumulative count 3. 7·CDF = ?
Slide 30 writes 1 × 7/16 = 0.43. The exact value is…
why: The slide truncates; it rounds to 0 either way.

q: Slide 29 image: cumulative count at r = 3 is 11 of 16. s_3?
Slide 29 image equalised: r = 4 maps to?
why: Cumulative 16/16 → 7.

q: 5×5 3-bit image with n_0 = 6. s_0 after HE?
MN = 4096; r=3 and r=4 (656 and 329 px) both map to 6. n(6) after HE?
why: Merged levels add their counts.

q: 4×4 image, L = 8, all 16 pixels have value 2. After HE they become?
why: CDF at 2 is 1, so s = 7.

q: Histogram specification needs as input…
choices: The image and a desired histogram
Only the image and its own histogram
Two images of exactly equal size
why: Its difficulty is constructing a meaningful target.

q: Histogram specification mapping:
why: Equalise input, then apply the inverse of the target's equalisation.

q: Slide 44 inverse LUT: equalised value s = 4 maps to z = ?
why: Closest G(z) to 4 is 4.8 at z = 6.

q: Slide 44 inverse LUT: s = 1 maps to z = ?
why: |1 − 0| < |1 − 2.6|, so z = 0 (slide column: 0).

q: Adding a constant to every pixel changes…
why: It shifts the histogram without stretching it.

q: 8-bit 250 + 20 with clamping?
why: Clamped to the max; 14 is what uint8 wrap-around gives.

q: 8-bit 50 − 100 with clamping?
why: Negative results clamp to 0.

q: Pixel 128 × 1.2, rounded?
Image subtraction is used for…
why: Medical blood-flow, PCB inspection, security monitoring.

q: NOT of 8-bit pixel 200?
200 AND 100 (bitwise)?
200 OR 100 (bitwise)?

why: Flips only the MSB: 200 − 128 = 72.

q: Why is XOR used to draw a mouse cursor?
choices: XOR is faster than AND or OR
why: A ⊕ k ⊕ k = A.

q: XOR of two equal pixel values gives…
why: Equal bits become 0, which is how XOR finds pixels of a given value.

q: A structuring element 'fits' an image at a position when:
choices: every 1 of the SE lies on an image 1
at least one 1 of the SE lies on a 1
every 0 of the SE lies on an image 0
the SE origin lies on an image 1
why: Fit = all SE 1s land on 1s (used by erosion). Hit = at least one does (used by dilation).

q: For grey-scale images, dilation replaces the anchor pixel with:
why: Slides 12-13: dilation is a local max, so bright regions grow.

q: For grey-scale images, erosion replaces the anchor pixel with:
choices: the weighted sum under the kernel
why: Slide 18: erosion computes a local minimum; bright areas thin, dark zones grow.

q: L10 slide 12 says dilation 'convolutes' the image with a kernel. What is it really?
choices: A max over the SE, so non-linear
A weighted sum, so it is linear
A min over the SE, so it is linear
A median over the SE, non-linear
why: Dilation is not convolution: the kernel only gives the neighbourhood, and the output is a max.

q: Which set expression is dilation A ⊕ B?
why: Dilation: positions where the reflected, shifted SE overlaps A in at least one element.

q: Which set expression is erosion A ⊖ B?
why: Erosion: positions where the shifted SE is entirely contained in A.

q: What is the reflection B̂ of a structuring element?
choices: B shifted by one pixel right
The complement of B in a window
why: B̂ = {w : w = −b, b ∈ B}: every point is mirrored through the origin (180° rotation).

q: Opening A ∘ B is defined as:
why: Opening = erosion followed by dilation with the same SE.

q: Closing A • B is defined as:
why: Closing = dilation followed by erosion with the same SE.

q: Which effect belongs to opening?
why: Opening smooths contours, breaks narrow isthmuses and eliminates thin protrusions; the rest are closing.

q: Which effect belongs to closing?
why: Closing fuses narrow breaks and long thin gulfs, eliminates small holes, fills gaps in the contour.

q: Which property holds for opening?
choices: A ∘ B is a subset of A
A is a subset of A ∘ B
why: Opening is anti-extensive (result ⊆ A); closing is extensive (A ⊆ result).

q: Applying an opening twice with the same SE gives:
choices: the same result as one opening
a result eroded twice as much
the closing of the image A
why: Opening and closing are idempotent: (A∘B)∘B = A∘B.

q: If C ⊆ D, which is true for closing?
why: Both opening and closing are increasing: they preserve set inclusion.

q: Boundary extraction β(A) is computed as:
why: The boundary is A minus its erosion. (A ⊕ B) − A would give an outer boundary instead.

q: The region-filling iteration in L10 is:
why: Grow the seed by dilation, then clip to the complement so it cannot cross the boundary. ∩ A is connected components.

q: Why does Gonzalez's region filling use the 3×3 cross, not the 3×3 square?
choices: A square leaks through diagonal gaps
A square never converges at all
A cross is faster to compute
A square removes the boundary A
why: The boundary is 8-connected; a square SE would step diagonally through it and flood the background.

q: The connected-component extraction iteration is:
why: Same loop as region filling but intersected with A, so growth stays inside the object.

q: The hit-or-miss transform A ⊛ B equals:
why: X must fit the object and its local background W − X must fit the complement; both erosions are intersected.

q: The morphological gradient is:
why: Slide 55: (A ⊕ B) − (A ⊖ B) highlights boundaries/edges.

q: The white top-hat transform is:
why: White top-hat = A − (A∘B), keeps small bright details. Black top-hat = (A•B) − A.

q: A d×d square is eroded by a centred (d/4)×(d/4) square SE. Result?
why: Erosion removes d/8 from each side: d − d/4 = 3d/4 (Fig. 9.6).

q: A d×d square is dilated by a centred (d/4)×(d/4) square SE. Side length?
why: Dilation adds d/8 on each side: d + d/4 = 5d/4 (Fig. 9.4).

q: A d×d square is eroded by a centred SE d/4 wide and d tall. Result?
why: Width shrinks to d − d/4 = 3d/4; height shrinks to d − d = 0, so a horizontal line (Fig. 9.6e).

q: Squares of side 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 15 are eroded by a 13×13 square. What survives?
why: Only squares ≥ 13 survive; 15 − 12 = 3. Dilating back with 13×13 restores 15×15 (Fig. 9.7).

q: A solid 5×5 block of 1s (background around it) is eroded by a 3×3 square. How many 1s remain?
why: Each side loses one pixel: a 3×3 block, 9 pixels.

q: A 4×4 block has a 1-pixel-wide line sticking out of one side. Opening with a 3×3 square gives:
choices: the 4×4 block with the line kept
only the 2×2 core of the block
an empty image with no pixels
why: Erosion leaves the 2×2 core and kills the line; dilation grows the core back to 4×4 only.

q: A 3×3 block of 1s has its centre pixel 0. Closing with a 3×3 square (block far from borders):
choices: fills the hole, giving a full 3×3
why: Dilation gives a 5×5 with no hole; erosion shrinks it back to a full 3×3.

q: Boundary extraction with a 3×3 square on a solid 5×5 block (background around it). Boundary pixel count?
why: Erosion leaves the 3×3 interior (9); 25 − 9 = 16 boundary pixels.

q: f = [3, 9, 3] and a flat 3-wide SE. Grey dilation at the middle sample is:
why: Dilation is the max of the window: max(3, 9, 3) = 9.

q: f = [3, 3, 9, 3, 3], flat 3-wide SE. The opening at the middle sample is:
why: Erosion gives [3,3,3,3,3]; dilating that gives 3: the narrow bright spike is removed.

q: L11 slide 60 says 'Opening filter: max → min'. Following L10, opening is:
why: L11 S60 swaps the names. L10 and Gonzalez: opening = erosion (min) then dilation (max).

q: Slide 14 multiplies I₀×M₀ … I₈×M₈ with no flip. Strictly, that is:
why: True convolution rotates the mask 180°. Identical for symmetric masks, different for Sobel or lopsided masks.

q: Correlate a unit impulse with w = [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]. The output is:
why: Correlation of an impulse gives the rotated mask; convolution gives the mask itself.

q: 1-D: f = [0, 1, 2] convolved (full) with w = [1, 1]. Result?
f = box of height 1 on [0,1], g = box of height ½ on [0,1]. Peak of f∗g?
why: The convolution is a triangle on [0, 2]: x/2 then 1 − x/2, peak ½ at x = 1.

q: Which is NOT one of the border-handling options on L11 slide 15?
choices: Mirror and double the edge pixels
why: Slide 15 lists zero-padding, starting at (1,1) (skipping borders), duplicating edges, and wrap-around.

q: Window [13 4 8; 2 9 6; 7 25 16]. Output of the 3×3 box filter?
Window [13 4 8; 2 9 6; 7 25 16] (L11 S55). Median filter output?
why: Sorted: 2 4 6 7 8 9 13 16 25; the 5th value is 8.

q: Window [13 4 8; 2 9 6; 7 25 16] with the Gaussian mask (1/16)[1 2 1; 2 4 2; 1 2 1]. Output?
Zero-padded 3×3 median at a corner pixel of an image that is all 10s. Output?
why: Five of the nine values are padding zeros, so the median (5th of 9) is 0.

q: A 3×3 box filter on a window of eight 10s and one 100 at the centre. Output?
why: (8·10 + 100)/9 = 180/9 = 20: the spike is spread, not removed.

q: 3×3 median on a window of eight 10s and one 255 (salt) at the centre. Output?
why: The extreme value sorts to the end; the 5th value is 10, so the impulse disappears.

q: Why is the median filter preferred to a low-pass filter for impulse noise?
choices: It removes impulses and keeps edges
It is linear, so it is faster
It sharpens the image as well
why: Slide 53: median removes impulse noise and preserves sharp edges; low-pass suits Gaussian noise.

q: The vector (colour) median outputs:
choices: the pixel with the smallest summed distance
the per-channel median of R, G and B
the pixel with the largest brightness
the average colour of the window
why: Slide 59: compute Distᵢ = Σⱼ |xᵢ − xⱼ| over R, G, B and return the xᵢ with the smallest Distᵢ.

q: A minimum filter removes which noise, and what happens to brightness?
why: Slide 60: min removes white spikes and lowers overall intensity; max removes dark spikes and raises it.

q: Why are min and max filters cascaded?
choices: Each alone fails on mixed salt and pepper
Each alone blurs edges too strongly
Each alone is too slow to compute
why: Slide 60: both fail on mixed impulse noise; cascading them can remove salt and pepper.

q: The deck prints a sharpening mask [1 −2 1; −1 5 −2; 1 −2 1]. Its weights sum to:
choices: 2, so it is a typo for −2 (sum 1)
1, so it is a valid mask as is
0, so it is a high-pass mask
9, so it must be divided by 9
why: 1−2+1−1+5−2+1−2+1 = 2. With −2 in place of −1 the sum is 1 like the other sharpening masks.

q: Unsharp masking, per L11, is:
why: Slide 21: subtract a low-pass filtered image from its original.

q: High-boost = A·Original − Lowpass. What happens when A = 1?
choices: It becomes a plain high-pass filter
It becomes a plain low-pass filter
why: Slide 21/24: A = 1 gives high-pass; A > 1 restores low-frequency content.

q: High-boost mask: −1/9 around a centre of w/9. For A = 2, w equals:
Centre 40, 3×3 mean 26.67. High-boost output for A = 1.2?
Mask (1/9)[−1 −1 −1; −1 8 −1; −1 −1 −1] on a flat patch of all 50s. Output?
why: The weights sum to 0, so any constant region gives 0.

q: Point mask [−1 −1 −1; −1 8 −1; −1 −1 −1] on 10s with centre 90. R = ?
Which line mask responds most to [0 0 9; 0 9 0; 9 0 0]?
why: The 9s run bottom-left to top-right, matching the +45° 2s: response 54; others give 0.

q: Homogeneity operator on [11 13 15; 16 11 11; 16 12 11]. Output?
why: Max |11 − neighbour| = |11 − 16| = 5 (L11 S34 worked example).

q: Difference operator on [20 22 40; 18 25 45; 19 21 50]. Output?
L11 slide 8 files Canny as 'second-order, Gaussian-based'. In fact Canny uses:
choices: the first derivative of a smoothed image
the median of a smoothed image
why: Canny = Gaussian smoothing + gradient (first derivative) + non-max suppression + hysteresis.

q: Per L11, the Roberts operator is:
choices: smallest in area and most noise-prone
largest in area and least noisy
why: Slide 38: Roberts has a smaller effective area and is more susceptible to noise.

q: Per L11 slide 38, the Sobel operator is more sensitive to:
why: Slide 38: Sobel more sensitive to diagonal edges; Prewitt more sensitive to vertical/horizontal.

q: Sobel Gx = 250, Gy = 110. Magnitude with |Gx| + |Gy| and with √(Gx² + Gy²)?
Sobel Gx on a vertical step: columns 10, 10, 90 (every row). Gx = ?
The deck's Sobel mask is [1 0 −1; 2 0 −2; 1 0 −1] instead of [−1 0 1; −2 0 2; −1 0 1]. Effect?
choices: Gx flips sign; magnitude is unchanged
Gx doubles; the direction is unchanged
Nothing changes in Gx or the magnitude
why: A negated mask negates the response: same |∇f|, direction rotated by 180°.

q: Compass gradient operators find edges by:
why: Slide 41: Prewitt, Kirsch, Robinson 3- and 5-level compass masks, eight orientations.

q: How does the Laplacian mark an edge?
choices: A local maximum of its value
A value above a fixed threshold
A local minimum of its value
why: Slide 45: the Laplacian output changes sign at edges; edges are zero crossings.

q: Which is NOT a disadvantage of the Laplacian listed on L11?
why: Slide 45 actually credits second derivatives with better localization; the other three are its listed drawbacks.
This mask = identity + 4-neighbour Laplacian: 30 + 40 = 70.

q: Ramp f = [10, 10, 20, 30, 30]. Second difference f[x+1] − 2f[x] + f[x−1] at x = 1, 2, 3?
why: x=1: 20 − 20 + 10 = 10; x=2: 30 − 40 + 10 = 0; x=3: 30 − 60 + 20 = −10. Double edge, zero crossing between.

q: Why apply a Gaussian before the Laplacian (LoG)?
choices: To reduce the Laplacian's noise sensitivity
To make the edges thicker and darker
To find the edge direction directly
To turn it into a first-derivative filter
why: Slide 48: LoG is a second-order edge detector less susceptible to noise because of the smoothing.

q: DoG approximates LoG well when the ratio of the two σ's is about:
why: Slide 49: σ₁ = 1.0, σ₂ = 1.6. (The slide writes σ₁/σ₂ = 1.6; it means σ₂/σ₁.)

q: L11 slide 4 splits filters into 'linear/smoothing' and 'frequency domain'. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Linear vs non-linear; spatial vs frequency
Linear vs frequency; spatial vs smoothing
Smoothing vs frequency; linear vs spatial
Median vs frequency; linear vs smoothing
why: Linear/non-linear is about what the filter does (median and min/max are non-linear); spatial/frequency is where you filter.

q: In L12, a 'pattern' is:
why: Slide 3: pattern = arrangement of descriptors (features); pattern class = family of patterns sharing properties.

q: In the sea bass vs salmon example, what does L12 conclude about length?
choices: Length alone is a poor feature
Length is the only feature needed
why: Slide 9: 'The length is a poor feature alone!' Lightness is tried next.

q: Why move the lightness threshold toward smaller values (slide 11)?
choices: To sell fewer sea bass as salmon
To sell more sea bass as salmon
To make both errors exactly equal
To ignore the cost of errors
why: The boundary is chosen to minimise cost: fewer sea bass classified as salmon. That is decision theory.

q: Adding the width to lightness makes the fish feature vector:
choices: xᵀ = [x₁, x₂] and the boundary a line
xᵀ = [x₁] and the boundary a point
xᵀ = [x₁, x₂, x₃] and the boundary a plane
xᵀ = [x₁, x₂] and the boundary a point
why: Slide 12: two features (lightness, width), so the decision boundary is a line in the 2-D plane.

q: What precaution does slide 14 give about adding more features?
why: A new feature should add new (uncorrelated) information, but noisy features can make results worse.

q: A boundary that perfectly separates all training fish raises the issue of:
choices: segmenting fish that overlap on the belt
the cost and resolution of the camera
the speed of the conveyor belt system
why: Slides 15-16: the aim is to classify novel input correctly; a too-complex boundary may not generalize.

q: What is the correct order of a pattern recognition system (L12)?
why: Slides 17-19: sensing → segmentation & grouping → feature extraction → classification → post-processing.

q: Which is NOT a step of the design cycle on L12 slide 20?
why: Design cycle: data collection, feature choice, model choice, training, evaluation (and computational complexity).

q: In supervised learning:
choices: a teacher gives a label or cost per pattern
the system forms natural clusters itself
no training data is used at all
only the class priors are known
why: Slide 28: supervised = teacher-provided labels/costs; unsupervised = the system forms natural groupings.

q: Structural pattern recognition represents data as:
why: Slide 30: structural PR uses discrete structures (grammars, graphs) with parsing/graph matching.

q: The 'reject class' is:
choices: for objects not in any known class
the class with the smallest prior
the class with the most samples
for objects on the boundary only
why: Slides 31, 36: a generic class for objects not in any of the designated known classes.

q: Using only [#holes, #strokes] from the slide-34 table, which characters cannot be told apart?
why: '1', '-' and '/' all have 0 holes and 1 stroke; other features (best axis, size) must separate them.

q: The nearest class mean classifier:
choices: picks the closest mean, rejects if too far
picks the class with the most samples
picks the nearest single training sample
picks the class with the largest prior
why: Slide 38: Euclidean distance to each class mean; choose the closest if close enough, otherwise reject.

q: Nearest mean fails when a class is multi-modal. The fix on slide 39:
choices: average the modes into one mean
why: Slide 39: if the modes are detected, two subclass mean vectors can be used.

q: Means m₁ = (1, 2), m₂ = (6, 1), m₃ = (3, 6). Nearest class to x = (4, 3)?
why: Squared distances 10, 8, 10: class 2 is closest.

q: Means m₁ = (4.3, 1.3), m₂ = (1.5, 0.3). The boundary d₁(x) − d₂(x) = 0 is:
Decision function d_j(x) = xᵀm_j − ½‖m_j‖². For m = (6, 1) and x = (4, 3), d = ?
With decision functions d_j(x) = xᵀm_j − ½‖m_j‖², the rule is:
choices: pick the d_j with the most terms
why: Maximising d_j is equivalent to minimising the Euclidean distance to m_j.

q: The minimum-distance boundary between two class means is:
choices: the perpendicular bisector of the means
the line joining the two means
a circle centred on one of the means
a parabola through both of the means
why: d_ij(x) = 0 is the set of points equidistant from m_i and m_j: the perpendicular bisector.

q: x = (5, 5); class mean (7, 2) with σ = (1, 4). Scaled Euclidean distance?
Why scale by each class's σ (slide 40)?
choices: It makes every distance a whole integer
It removes the need for any class means
It turns k-NN into a nearest-mean rule
why: A point at the top of a widely spread class can be nearer its mean once each axis is divided by that class's σ.

q: The nearest neighbour classifier:
choices: keeps all samples, uses the nearest one
keeps one mean vector per class only
keeps only the class prior probabilities
why: Slide 41: keep all training samples, assign the class of the nearest neighbour; extends to k-NN.

q: q = (3, 3). Neighbours by distance: R (1), B (1.41), B (2), R (2.24), R (2.83). 1-NN, 3-NN, 5-NN give:
why: k=1: R. k=3: R,B,B → B. k=5: R,B,B,R,R → R. The answer depends on k.

q: For a 2-class k-NN vote, why choose an odd k?
why: With two classes an even k can split evenly; an odd k always gives a majority.

q: In Bayes' rule P(ωᵢ|x) = p(x|ωᵢ)P(ωᵢ)/p(x), P(ωᵢ) is the:
why: Slide 42: class-conditional p(x|ωᵢ), a priori P(ωᵢ), unconditional p(x).

q: In Bayes' rule, p(x) in the denominator is:
choices: Σⱼ p(x|ωⱼ)P(ωⱼ), the same for all classes
the prior of the most likely class
the posterior of the chosen class
why: p(x) = Σ p(x|ωⱼ)P(ωⱼ) is common to every class, so it does not change which class wins.

q: P(salmon) = 0.6, P(bass) = 0.4, p(bright|salmon) = 0.2, p(bright|bass) = 0.7. P(bass | bright)?
Priors 0.5, 0.3, 0.2; likelihoods 0.1, 0.4, 0.6. The evidence p(x) is:
Slide 42 says use Bayes' rule 'if all classes are disjoint'. The proper condition is:
why: Exclusive and exhaustive classes let p(x) expand into Σ p(x|ωⱼ)P(ωⱼ).

q: 50 salmon (45 correct) and 50 sea bass (40 correct) are tested. Error rate?
why: Errors 5 + 10 = 15 of 100 = 15% (accuracy 85%).

q: An m × n template must reach every border pixel. Padding on top/bottom and left/right?
why: Fig. 12.8 (slide 35): pad (m−1)/2 and (n−1)/2 so the template centre can sit on any image pixel.
